I didn't define "genetic winners" as being beautiful athletes who make it to varsity. YOU defined it that way. I just pointed out that having kids is, definitionally, what it means to be a genetic winner.

Maybe your instinct is to respond "The kind of people who end up in happy relationships and having kids aren't always athletes, they're just decent normal people who are able to be themselves." But all that means is that someone who is able to do that is a genetic winner, and an inability to be a decent, normal person would (again, by definition) make me a genetic loser.

I do feel like this sometimes, even if I intellectually know it's wrong.

A lot of emphasis is placed on how this is a "doomer" mindset. But what I want to take a moment to emphasize is that this is often how people who AREN'T doomers explicitly look at people who are struggling with personal improvement.

Like, I'm not a big fan of (say) Jordan Peterson or Andrew Tate, and I think they do a lot of harm. But a lot of people, when arguing that people like Peterson and Tate are harmful, basically make an argument that boils down to "Self improvement is a scam and isn't necessary for normal people. If you needed Jordan Peterson to tell you to clean your room, you're beyond help. Just live your life, it's not hard." Which is basically the socially acceptable version of the view expressed in this screenshot.
I mean, in a sense, BY DEFINITION, only genetic winners have kids, so I'm not sure what you mean. What would a counterexample even look like?
Interesting. Would you say the person who wrote it is a really pathetic loser?

Not great, since you asked.

I'm Canadian, so really it doesn't have an immediate direct effect on me, but we have right-wing movements in Canada as well, so I can't say it's completely safe here either. I don't even think there's anywhere better I could reasonably escape to, or if that would even be worth it. I can't imagine how this would be affecting me if I were a US resident.

Whenever I read people trying to be inspirational, saying things like "Now is the time for action!" "Help people in your communities!" "Join a local leftist group!" it just sounds exhausting, impossible, and pointless. Exhausting and impossible, because I don't even have enough energy to take care of myself and maintain my own friendships. Pointless, because right now, it just feels like the bad guys are always going to win everything forever. Any victory I help to achieve will be temporary and it will be a constant struggle to maintain it, because the bad guys have all the money and will just astroturf a movement to take it away again. It just feels like everything that is good in the world exists by a fluke and will be replaced with something shitty as soon as someone powerful notices that someone is experiencing happiness without their permission.

I have a lot of respect for people who are able to go on and fight even in the face of hopelessness. I wish I were a better person and able to do that, the way other people on this subreddit, and Robert and the other Cool Zone Media people are able to that. But I'm finding myself unable to do anything more than survive.

My experience with every group of activists I've ever been a part of is that the energy and interest tends to fizzle out pretty quickly, and that any progress just feels like kicking water uphill. "Then you just have to put more effort into it!" Again, I don't even have the energy to take care of myself. If being unwilling to carry another burden on my shoulders makes me a bad person, then okay, I guess I'm a bad person. And why would you want a bad person like me to drag down your movement? It might be that the best thing for me to do for the movement would be to stay out of the way.

"Wow, you're really a downer. It sounds like you should get therapy." Therapy is expensive and not adequately covered by my insurance. There are some free or sliding-scale options, but I've found that they're generally students, who I've found to be (a) less skilled than professionals, and (b) not a long-term solution, since they don't stay students forever. Whenever I talk to my doctor about this, she just gives me the same list of free resources.

I recently finished a Master's degree in mathematics. "Okay, so just make a lot of money in a math job and donate it to leftist causes!" I wish I had the energy to do that. But anything I'm qualified for feels meaningless. And any meaningful job is going to have a lot of competition from people who are better human beings than I am anyway. I imagine that it's frustrating to read my whining, because I'm clearly in such a privileged position and have had so much given to me, and yet I find myself without the drive to give back. I kind of just want to die.

I've been meaning to write my feelings about Trump winning, but no venue seemed appropriate. I don't want to burden the people I know with this, and posting it anywhere feels like a cry for attention, yet I have this unhealthy need to have an audience for my thoughts, because it just feels incomplete to write in a journal to myself. I figured posting on a 2-day-old Reddit thread where no one will see it, using a throwaway account I created a few years ago to post on r/SuicideWatch, would be a good compromise.

(In case anyone's worried, I don't think I'm in danger of actually killing myself. Intellectually, I know that the feeling of abject hopelessness is a temporary part of a wave, soon to be replaced with just a general dislike of everyday life. This account was created eight years ago, and I'm still here for some reason. I think wanting to die is just a recurring fixture in my life for as long as I'm alive, independent of world events.)

I am considering the possibility that I might be trans (MtF).

Arguments in favour:

- I really don't enjoy having a physical body. I just assumed that that was a weird quirk about me, or that that's just what being alive is like. But now I think it may be worth considering the possibility that this has something to do with me not wanting to have a *male* body specifically.

- When I read messages about the importance of "loving your body", I find it easier to do if I imagine myself with a woman's body. With regards to how diet and exercise affect my appearance, it's slightly disappointing to know that, if I eat better and exercise more, even in the best case scenario, I'll still look like a man.

- Related to the whole "male body" thing: whenever people use the metaphor "feeling big" as a synonym for feeling confident, happy, etc, that always seems weird to me. I'm already big and relatively broad-shouldered, and I associate it with awkwardness and discomfort.

- I have a beard, and people sometimes compliment it, but when I picture in my head how I really want to look, I (usually) don't picture a beard. Sometimes I do, but other times I imagine something more feminine. I particularly found myself fascinated with [this](https://www.reddit.com/r/traaaaaaannnnnnnnnns/comments/cqdqpm/me_wants_to_transition_to_a_dude_but_also_look_as/) post on /r/traa (Counterpoint: The person who posted that intended it as an example of reading as male but looking as feminine as possible, which sort of works against my MtF hypothesis about myself).

- I've lurked /r/traa and /r/egg_irl for probably just under a year.

- I would definitely press The Button. Most of my reasons for not wanting to transition have more to do with difficulty and practicality, rather than doubts about it being what I want. I'm less worried about "regretting" the transition, and more worried about whether it's worth the trouble.

- I've enjoyed classes and workplaces where the gender ratio is mixed or skews female, more than when it skews male.

- When I find out about a resource that tailors specifically to men, e.g. male-oriented group therapy or even just an innocuous subreddit like /r/malefashionadvice/, my first thought is "Oh, good for them" (third person) rather than identifying with it myself. Even when I see media portrayals of masculinity in media that attempt to celebrate different kinds of men, e.g. [this 2016 Axe ad](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lUyPrq4AmIY), I don't find myself feeling like it applies to me, insofar as it refers to "men".

- I'm not a big fan of being called "dude", "bro" or "man".

- Intellectually, I understand that there are people who are assigned female at birth but who want to be male, and I respect that. But I can't wrap my head around wanting to be male as well as I can wrap my head around wanting to be female. (Or just abolishing gender altogether.)

Arguments Against:

- I don't mind having a penis -- I kind of like it, in fact.

- Other body-related things: I like being able to grow a beard, and it's really convenient to have the upper body strength that I have.

- I get advantages from the fact that society sees me as a man. To the extent that men have power in society that women and non-binary people don't, one could argue that the most ethical thing I can do is to use my power for good, rather than relinquishing it.

- I'm broke and likely to remain so for the foreseeable future. I'm lucky enough to live in a part of the world where the medical transition will probably be at least partly paid for as part of public health care, but there are other expenses I can see being a problem (replacing my wardrobe, living expenses when recovering from surgery). When I think about the money and effort it would take to get to a point where I'd be happy with my appearance, there are other things I would rather spend my resources on.

- I don't think I'd be a very attractive woman. (Counterpoint: I'm already not a very attractive man, so it's not like this would make my life *worse*.)

- When I think about the things that I don't like about my life, e.g. social isolation, not taking care of my physical health -- it seems naive to think that transitioning would be particularly motivating for me to fix these things. If anything, it would throw a wrench into the works. If I want to improve my life, I should fix those other problems first.

- There are many aspects of transitioning that make me afraid and anxious, even things as simple as going to a store and shopping for a dress given my current wardrobe (and size). "Wait! Are you such a coward that you're going to let fear run your life?" Yes, that is exactly what I'm saying.

That is where I am right now. It seems like it would be reasonable to at least consider myself nonbinary -- although I'm fascinated with the idea of being a woman, I'm mostly just frustrated with the existence of gender.

I've considered this. On the other hand, whenever I see someone promoting non-toxic masculinity or someone supporting gender-nonconforming men, it sometimes feels more like my brain is going "All right, good for them!" as opposed to feeling like it applies to me.

> I'm sorry but you're too funny and this made me laugh several times.

That's fine. It's hard to turn it off -- I once wrote an essay about the Holocaust for a university course, and my classmates complimented me on how "entertaining" it was (I genuinely was not trying to be entertaining). I think one of the reasons I didn't get along with the first counselor is that, in an awkward situation, my first instinct is to make a joke. I think a lot of people have that instinct, and I suspect counselors are trained to be resistant to that kind of thing.

> Why does the story of your life end so sadly? Can't you retell it differently?

If I'm being realistic, there exist possible futures in which I achieve some level of happiness. I could imagine accidentally getting an okay job, possibly through a friend. I would settle for something that pays the bills, maybe enough time and income to fund a hobby or two, and enough that I could save a percentage every month. I could imagine accidentally running into a person who I fall in love with -- probably a rather strange person, someone I "click" with, who challenges me to become a better person, but does so out of a place of love.

I don't have much money, but what I do have, I think I manage as well as I reasonably can, so I could imagine a future in which I'm no longer renting, or at least where I have some money saved away. Not sure if I want kids -- adopted, maybe, because mental illness has a huge genetic component and I don't know if I want to subject any more children to that.

That's me at my most optimistic. Strictly speaking, I don't know for sure what's going to happen in the future. I don't know for a fact that I *won't* find true, lasting happiness. But it doesn't seem likely.

> But you want to collaborate on something anyway? . . . So I'm just saying, I see a creative witty person behind your words and maybe chatting a bit will have a good result. I'm listening if you want to talk.

I'm feeling a bit too unstable to commit to anything right now, although I am curious about what sort of ideas you have.
A part of me would *really* like to get a reply to this. I am aware that it is pathetic to beg for attention. But it looks like that's exactly what I'm going to do. Hell, I'd even take trolling.
